# Isaiah 52 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Isaiah 52 falls into two major sections: (1) **vv. 1–12**, a prophetic call for Zion to awake and rejoice because God is about to redeem and restore her; and (2) **vv. 13–15**, the opening of the fourth "Servant Song" (continuing through Isaiah 53), which introduces the suffering and exaltation of the Servant of the LORD. Commentators across traditions agree that the chapter break here is unfortunate — 52:13–15 is the prologue to Isaiah 53 (Precept Austin; JFB).

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-53-commentary ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm

---

## v. 1 — "Awake, awake, clothe yourself with strength…"

**Traditional Reading:** This is the third "Awake, awake!" in this section of Isaiah. The first (51:9) asked the LORD's arm to put on strength; the second (51:17) called Jerusalem to remember God's promises. Now Zion herself is summoned to rise from dejection and clothe herself in strength — not her own, but the strength God supplies (Guzik/Enduring Word). Ellicott notes the repetition is a "subtle touch of art" marking continuity of thought: Zion the castaway is summoned to highest glory, putting on garments befitting a "priestly queen of cities" (cf. Exodus 28:2, the priestly garments). JFB calls "strength" her "adornment," parallel to "beautiful garments."

**"Uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter you":** Ellicott and JFB both point to Revelation 21:2, 27 — this is a prophecy never yet fulfilled in history, pointing to the heavenly Jerusalem. The Cambridge Bible clarifies that "uncircumcised and unclean" refers to the destroyers and wasters desecrating her, not foreigners generally (cf. Joel 3:17). Gill (Baptist) argues this cannot refer to literal Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, since Antiochus Epiphanes, Pompey, and the Romans did later enter it — therefore it must refer to the church in the latter-day glory or the New Jerusalem.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/52.htm

---

## v. 2 — "Shake off your dust! Rise up and sit on your throne…"

**Traditional Reading:** "Dust" is the posture of mourning (Job 2:12–13). Ellicott notes that "sit down" implies sitting on a throne — a deliberate contrast with Babylon's humiliation in Isaiah 47:1 ("sit in the dust… sit in silence"). JFB agrees: "arise, and sit — namely, in a more dignified place: on a divan or a throne" (Lowth). The "chains from your neck" represent the yoke of captivity. The Cambridge Bible adds a textual note: the alternative reading "the bands of thy neck are loosed" represents the Hebrew consonantal text, but the Qerê (marginal reading) supported by ancient versions is preferred.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm

---

## v. 3 — "You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed."

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott explains that the people had complained that Jehovah had "sold them" (Psalm 44:12). God answers: "There was no real sale, only a temporary transfer, and therefore Jehovah can redeem you at His own pleasure." Guzik (Enduring Word) says Israel tragically sold herself for nothing by chasing after other gods; yet God's mercy answered with redemption "without money" — but this does not mean redemption cost nothing; the rest of the chapter shows the cost is paid by Another. JFB adds a spiritual application: as Israel was "sold under sin" gratuitously (Romans 7:14), so she shall be redeemed gratuitously (cf. Isaiah 55:1). Gill applies it to spiritual redemption from sin: "not without the price of the precious blood of the Lamb, but without such corruptible things as silver and gold" (1 Peter 1:18).

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/52.htm

---

## v. 4 — "At first My people went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them without cause."

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott stresses the "unprovoked character" of the oppression in both Egypt and Assyria (Sargon/Sennacherib). He notes Assyria may be used in its wider sense including Babylon. JFB says the reasoning is: "Remember how I delivered you from Egypt and the Assyrian; what, then, is to prevent Me from delivering you out of Babylon?" The Cambridge Bible renders "at the first" (R.V.) as "at the outset of its history," and explains "without cause" as meaning the oppressors had acquired no right over Israel by any service rendered to Jehovah.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm

---

## v. 5 — "Those who rule them taunt… and My name is blasphemed continually all day long."

**Traditional Reading:** The Cambridge Bible explains "What have I here?" as expressing "a strong sense of incongruity between what is and what ought to be." The calamities of Israel were attributed by the heathen to their God's impotence, thus blaspheming His name — a thought frequently expressed by Ezekiel (cf. Ezekiel 36:20ff.). The words are cited in Romans 2:24. JFB notes that God's reason for delivering His people is not their goodness but "for the sake of His holy name" (Ezekiel 20:9, 14). Guzik says the nations' blasphemy was worse than their oppression of the people, and God declares: "I can abide with My name being blasphemed continually every day among the nations. Just let it be known and praised among My people."

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 6 — "Therefore My people will know My name… Here I am!"

**Traditional Reading:** JFB sees this as fulfilled when Christ shall reveal Himself to Israel "sensibly" — the only means whereby their obstinate unbelief shall be overcome (Psalm 102:16; Zechariah 12:10; 14:5). The Cambridge Bible explains "know My name" means knowing by experience what God's name imports — similar to Ezekiel's "they shall know that I am Jehovah." The final "Here I am" (or "Behold, it is I") simply repeats the sense of the preceding clause. Guzik stresses the tragedy that God's own people in Isaiah's day did not know the LORD had spoken through His Word — something expected among the nations but never among God's people.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 7 — "How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news…"

**Traditional Reading:** This is among the most-quoted verses in the New Testament (Romans 10:15; cf. Ephesians 6:15). Ellicott notes the image is reproduced from Isaiah 40:9 — there Zion herself was the herald; here heralds are seen coming to Zion, their feet beautiful like an antelope (Song of Solomon 2:8–9; Nahum 1:15). Guzik says feet speak of "activity, motion, and progress" — those actively moving in preaching the gospel have beautiful feet. The Cambridge Bible explains the *měbassçr* ("bringer of good tidings") is an ideal creation of the prophet's imagination — an "evangelist" whose single function is announcing to Zion that her God has become King. "Your God reigns" is better rendered "Your God has become King" — He has established His everlasting kingdom (cf. Psalm 93:1; 97:1).

JFB says this applies "only partially" to the return from Babylon; fully and antitypically, it is the Gospel (Luke 2:10–11), "beginning at Jerusalem" (Luke 24:47).

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 8 — "Listen! Your watchmen lift up their voices… For every eye will see when the LORD returns to Zion."

**Traditional Reading:** The Cambridge Bible argues the watchmen are not prophets (as in Isaiah 56:10; Habakkuk 2:1) but literal watchmen on the city walls — prophets are no longer needed once the herald has arrived and Jehovah Himself is at hand. They are the first to see and announce the King's approach. Ellicott agrees: sentinels on watch-towers see the heralds and sing for joy.

On **"eye to eye"**: This is the main translation dispute in this verse. The Cambridge Bible insists the phrase in Hebrew "has not the sense of harmony and unity which it has come to bear in English." It means "eye to eye do they look upon Jehovah's return to Zion" — i.e., they see Jehovah visibly, as clearly as when two people look each other in the face (cf. Numbers 14:14). JFB (citing Gesenius) supports this: "close at hand, and so clearly," comparing Numbers 14:14 "face to face." Guzik, however, follows the traditional English sense of harmonious agreement: watchmen "see eye to eye" meaning they agree in their joyful singing.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 9 — "Break forth in joy, sing together, O ruins of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem."

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott observes that the history of the return under Ezra seems "a somewhat poor and prosaic fulfilment" of this glorious vision — the prophet idealises the return and connects it "unconsciously, it may be, with another city than the earthly Jerusalem." Guzik identifies two bases for joy: the LORD's word of comfort and His work of redemption. The Cambridge Bible points to the echo of Isaiah 44:23 and 51:3.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm

---

## v. 10 — "The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations; all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God."

**Traditional Reading:** "Bared His holy arm" is a Hebrew idiom: the warrior preparing for action throws off his mantle and tucks up his sleeve, leaving the outstretched arm free (Ellicott, JFB, Cambridge). Guzik, citing Bultema, says it derives "from rolling up long, loose sleeves before starting to work." Ellicott contrasts the metaphor with Psalm 74:11 ("Why do You withdraw Your hand, even Your right hand?"). Guzik notes that the thought begun at Isaiah 51:9 ("Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD!") is completed here: the arm of the LORD has acted. All nations see this as a witness and testimony — not just for those immediately rescued.

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 11 — "Depart, depart, go out from there! Touch no unclean thing… purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD."

**Traditional Reading:** A call to the exiles to leave Babylon — both literal and spiritual (cf. 2 Corinthians 6:14–18; Revelation 18:4). Ellicott explains they are not to plunder but to bring only "the vessels of Jehovah" — the gold and silver taken from the temple, which Cyrus restored (Ezra 1:7). The bearers were Levites. The Cambridge Bible notes the unusual stress on ceremonial purity here: the exiles are to "purify themselves" as those in a religious procession.

On **"vessels of the LORD"**, there is a translation debate: some commentators render "armour-bearers" of Jehovah (Ellicott mentions this; so does the Cambridge Bible, citing Cheyne). The imagery would be military — the people as armour-bearers for the divine King (1 Kings 14:27–28). But most traditional translations and commentaries prefer "vessels" = temple vessels.

JFB applies this spiritually: long residence in Babylon made many loath to leave it; so it is with mystical Babylon. Guzik: "2 Timothy 2:21 has a wonderful promise for those vessels of the LORD who pursue purity."

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 12 — "For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste, for the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard."

**Traditional Reading:** A deliberate contrast with the exodus from Egypt, when Israel left in haste (Exodus 12:11, 33, 39; Deuteronomy 16:3). This departure will be calm, dignified, and secure. Ellicott: "Jehovah would still be once more both the vanguard and the rear-guard of the great procession." JFB sees significance in the presence of Jehovah both before and behind — a complete divine protection. Guzik says there is "a sense of peace in the glorious work of the LORD, not a striving in haste or by flight."

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## vv. 13–15 — The Fourth Servant Song: Introduction

All consulted sources agree vv. 13–15 form the prologue to the great Suffering Servant passage of Isaiah 53. The Cambridge Bible calls it "a prelude to ch. 53, being a summary of what is there described in detail." JFB states bluntly: "Here the fifty-third chapter ought to begin." Precept Austin describes Isaiah 52:13–15 as "a summary and preview of the humiliation and exaltation of the Servant" and notes the five-stanza structure spanning 52:13–53:12.

---

## v. 13 — "Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted."

**Traditional Reading:** All Protestant commentators consulted see this as a clear Messianic prophecy fulfilled in Jesus. Guzik notes that while many are called "servant" in Isaiah (Isaiah himself, Eliakim, David, Israel), the context here — and Matthew's application in Matthew 8:16–17 and 12:16–21 — demonstrates this is Jesus. The phrase "My Servant" refers back to the Servant of Isaiah 42:1 and 49:3, 6.

On **"deal prudently" / "prosper"**: Ellicott says the verb means "prospering" (as in Joshua 1:8; Jeremiah 10:21), and the same verb describes the "righteous branch" in Jeremiah 23:5. The Cambridge Bible prefers "shall prosper" (R.V. margin): "the primary idea… is no doubt 'wisdom'… but it also includes the success which is the normal result of wise action." JFB (with Gesenius) renders "prosper"; Hengstenberg combines both: "shall reign well."

On **"raised and lifted up and highly exalted"**: Ellicott notes this phrase impressed itself on Christ's mind through the LXX regarding His crucifixion (John 3:14; 8:28; 12:32) and on the Apostles regarding His ascension (Acts 2:33; Philippians 2:9). The Cambridge Bible observes these are the same words used of Jehovah's throne in Isaiah 6:1 and of Jehovah Himself in Isaiah 57:15.

Guzik stresses that God announces the Servant's triumph *first* — "before any of His suffering is announced, His glorious triumph is assured."

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-53-commentary

---

## v. 14 — "Just as many were appalled at Him—His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man…"

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott notes this "conflicts strangely with the type of pure and holy beauty with which Christian art has made us familiar." Early Christian art prior to Constantine often depicted Christ as worn and emaciated. Guzik applies this to the beating Jesus endured: His face was beaten so severely He "hardly looked like a man" (cf. Luke 22:63–64). He speculates that the marred visage may have remained after the resurrection, noting the disciples' hesitation to recognize Him (Luke 24:16; John 20:14; 21:4, 12) — though these scars "will only increase His glory and beauty to our eyes, standing as badges of His matchless love."

The Cambridge Bible explains the grammar: vv. 14–15 form a single compound sentence. The protasis ("Just as many were astonished at you") is followed by intervening parenthesis ("His visage was so marred…"), and the apodosis comes in v. 15 ("so shall He sprinkle…").

JFB: The marring was so severe that Castalio translated "so that it was no longer that of a man" (cf. Psalm 22:6). "The more perfect we may suppose the 'body prepared' (Hebrews 10:5) for Him by God, the sadder by contrast was the 'marring' of His visage and form."

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## v. 15 — "So He will sprinkle many nations…"

### The Translation Debate over "Sprinkle"

This is the most significant translation dispute in the chapter. The Hebrew verb *yazzeh* is universally used in the Old Testament for sprinkling blood (priestly expiation — Leviticus 4:6; 16:18–19) or water (purification — Ezekiel 36:25). Most traditional translations (KJV, NKJV, BSB, NASB) render "sprinkle." Ellicott defends this reading: "The 'sprinkling' is that of the priest who cleanses the leper" — done by Him who was Himself "counted as a leper 'smitten of God'" (Isaiah 53:4). He traces an echo of the words in Ezekiel 36:25 ("sprinkle clean water") and the "blood of sprinkling" of Hebrews 10:22 and 12:24.

JFB likewise defends "sprinkle": many were astonished at Him; so many nations shall be cleansed by His priestly work. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary links it to Numbers 19:17–19 and Titus 3:5–6 — cleansing by His blood.

**However**, the Cambridge Bible argues that the traditional rendering is "inadmissible on grammatical grounds" because the verb always means "to sprinkle (a liquid), not to besprinkle (a person or thing)." It notes the LXX renders "many nations shall marvel" (θαυμάσονται), and the R.V. margin gives "so will he startle many nations." The idea: as many were astonished at His disfigurement, so many nations will be startled at His exaltation. "Most modern writers agree in this explanation."

Guzik (Enduring Word) retains the traditional "sprinkle" reading: "Sprinkling is often associated with cleansing from sin in the Old Testament… His saving, cleansing work will extend far beyond Israel to many nations."

### "Kings will shut their mouths"

Both traditions agree this represents reverent, awed silence. Ellicott: "the reverence… of silent wonder at the change which has passed over the suffering Servant" (cf. Job 29:9; 40:4). JFB: "Men were dumb with the amazement of scorn at one marred more than the lowest of men, yet the highest: even kings shall be dumb with awe and veneration."

### "What they have not been told they will see"

The Cambridge Bible says this refers to the exaltation of the Servant as "an event of which they had received no announcement beforehand" — or one "the like of which had never been known."

**Sources:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The Identity of the Servant (vv. 13–15)
Across the consulted sites, **all Protestant traditions represented here agree** that the Servant is the Messiah, Jesus Christ. The main alternative — that the Servant is the nation of Israel collectively or the pious remnant — is noted by JFB as a Jewish and some critical-scholar interpretation, which JFB refutes: "An individual is plainly described: he suffers voluntarily, innocently, patiently, and as the efficient cause of the righteousness of His people, which holds good of none other but Messiah." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that some ancient Jews, unable to reconcile Messianic glory with humiliation, developed a "two-Messiah philosophy" (Messiah ben Joseph who suffers, Messiah ben David who conquers).

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/52.htm

### Timing of Fulfillment (vv. 1–12)
- **Premillennial/Dispensational** (Guzik/Enduring Word, JFB): The ultimate fulfillment of vv. 1–6 is in the "very last days" when Christ reigns from Jerusalem and the uncircumcised literally never enter the holy city again (cf. Revelation 21:27; Zechariah 14:21).
- **Amillennial/Covenantal** (implied by Ellicott and Cambridge): The vision finds its fulfillment in the church age and ultimately the heavenly Jerusalem — the earthly return under Ezra being a "prosaic fulfilment" that the prophet "idealises."
- Gill (Baptist) applies v. 1 directly to the church in gospel times, not literal Jerusalem, identifying "the uncircumcised" as Papists who will no longer persecute the true church.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/52.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/52.htm

### "Eye to eye" (v. 8)
- Traditional English/evangelical reading (Guzik): Watchmen agree in harmony — "seeing eye to eye" as the English idiom means.
- Scholarly reading (Ellicott, Cambridge, JFB/Gesenius): They see Jehovah "eye to eye" = visibly, face to face, at close range — the Hebrew does not carry the English idiomatic sense of agreement.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm

### "Vessels of the LORD" (v. 11)
- Majority view (Ellicott, JFB, Cambridge, Guzik): The temple vessels carried back by priests/Levites (Ezra 1:7–11).
- Minority view (Cheyne, mentioned by Ellicott and Cambridge): "Armour-bearers" of Jehovah — a military metaphor for the whole people as the King's retinue (1 Kings 14:27–28).

### "Sprinkle" vs. "Startle" (v. 15)
As detailed above, this is the major exegetical divide, falling largely along lines of older translations (KJV tradition = "sprinkle") versus modern critical scholarship (R.V. margin, Cambridge, LXX = "startle/marvel"). Conservative evangelical commentators (Guzik, JFB, Ellicott, Garner-Howes Baptist) retain "sprinkle" for its atonement theology.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
The Cambridge Bible (representing a more critical approach) questions whether vv. 3–6 were the "original sequel" to vv. 1–2, noting the sudden change in form and subject. It also speculates about whether the Servant was originally an individual Israelite (perhaps the prophet himself, or Jeremiah) — though it acknowledges that "the whole conception… makes the prophecy the most remarkable anticipation in the Old Testament of the 'sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.'"

On v. 7, the Cambridge Bible identifies the *měbassçr* not as a literal person but "an ideal creation of the writer's mind" — the herald figure fluctuates between an individual and a company.

**Source:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/52.htm

### Catholic Readings
I was unable to access Catholic commentary pages (newadvent.org, catholic.com) due to search/fetch limits. Catholic exegesis traditionally reads Isaiah 52–53 Christologically, as seen in the Vulgate's *asperget* ("he shall sprinkle") in v. 15 — a reading that undergirds the theology of Christ's atoning blood applied to the nations, deeply connected to the Mass and sacraments. This is consistent with the traditional Protestant reading on this point.

### Orthodox Readings
I was unable to access Orthodox pages (oca.org) due to limits. Orthodox tradition likewise reads the Servant Songs Christologically, often seeing in v. 7 the apostolic preaching of the Gospel and in vv. 13–15 the paradox of Christ's kenosis and glorification (Philippians 2:5–11).

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching
No specific prosperity/Word of Faith/hyper-grace interpretations of Isaiah 52 surfaced in the pages consulted. Guzik (Enduring Word) — who is charismatic in orientation — applies v. 1 as a call for the church to "awake out of sleep" from "general carnal security and spiritual drowsiness," emphasising putting on strength through Christ, not through human effort. His reading of v. 3 ("redeemed without money" but "a cost paid by another") is entirely consistent with substitutionary atonement and does not reflect prosperity-gospel or hyper-grace distinctives.

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-52/

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **God's initiative in redemption** (vv. 1–6): God acts for His Name's sake, not because Israel earned it. The "without money" redemption points toward grace.
2. **The Gospel mission** (vv. 7–10): The herald with beautiful feet proclaims "Your God reigns" — the heart of the good news. Paul applies this directly to gospel preachers (Romans 10:15).
3. **Separation and purity** (vv. 11–12): Those who carry the LORD's vessels must be clean — a call to holy living, applied in the New Testament to separation from the world (2 Corinthians 6:17).
4. **The suffering and exalted Servant** (vv. 13–15): The paradox of the gospel: the marred, disfigured One will sprinkle/startle the nations, and kings will fall silent before Him.
